title: Document and Record Control Procedure
summary: How ISMS documents and records are identified, approved, versioned, published, acknowledged, stored, retained and disposed of in Verity.
content_html:
Document and Record Control Procedure

Document Type: Procedure

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the document owner>Version: <Version number>
Effective Date:<Date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review:<Date>Next Review: <Date>

Purpose

This procedure sets out how {{company_name}} creates, approves, publishes, reviews, stores, retains and disposes of the documents and records of its information security management system (ISMS), so that staff always work from the current approved version and records can be trusted as evidence. It supports ISO/IEC 27001 clauses 7.5.1, 7.5.2 and 7.5.3 and controls A.5.1, A.5.33 and A.5.37.

Scope

  • Documents: policies, procedures, standards, plans, operating procedures and runbooks, the ISMS scope statement and the Statement of Applicability.
  • Records: outputs that prove an activity happened, such as risk assessments, audit reports, management review minutes, training and acknowledgement records, incident records and evidence attached to controls.
  • Documents of external origin that the ISMS relies on, such as contracts, supplier assurance reports, certificates and published standards.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • ISMS owner (<Name and job title of the ISMS owner>): owns this procedure and the list of required documents, and confirms each year that every required document exists, is current and has an owner.
  • Document owners: draft, maintain and review their documents, choose approvers and run acknowledgement campaigns.
  • Approvers: review drafts assigned to them in an approval tier and approve or reject them.
  • Record owners: the owners of the controls and processes that produce records, who file them in the agreed place.
  • All staff: use only the published version and acknowledge documents when asked.

Procedure

1. Required documents

  1. The Verity Documents register is the list of controlled ISMS documents. The ISMS owner adds every document and record that clauses 4 to 10 of ISO/IEC 27001 require, using the clause requirements in the Verity ISO 27001 framework as the checklist (for example the scope, the security policy, the risk method and its results, the Statement of Applicability, objectives, competence records, monitoring results, the audit programme and its results, management review results and corrective actions). The ISMS owner also adds every document needed because of the Statement of Applicability, legal and contractual obligations or customer commitments. A required record kept in another Verity module, such as the risk register, Frameworks or Tasks, is listed with that location.
  2. Each document has one named owner. When an owner leaves or changes role, ownership is reassigned as part of offboarding before their access is removed.
  3. Documents kept outside Verity, such as runbooks in <Tool where operating procedures and runbooks are kept, for example the engineering wiki>, are listed in the Documents register with their location and owner and follow this procedure.
  4. The ISMS scope statement and the Statement of Applicability are held in Verity Frameworks, and the Statement's XLSX export shows the scope statement at the top. Both are approved together as set out in the Risk Assessment and Treatment Methodology, not through the approval tiers in section 3. Both are listed in the Documents register with that location.

2. Identification and format

  1. Verity records the authoritative version, approvers, approval dates and next review date of every document. The header table at the top repeats the title, document type, owner, version, effective date, approver and review dates for readers of exported or printed copies, and the owner updates it in each new version before approval. Where the header and the Verity record differ, the Verity record applies.
  2. Titles are unique in the register. Each document ends with a revision history listing version, date, author and a description of the change.
  3. Documents are written in plain language in <Language or languages of controlled documents>. Diagrams and records attached as evidence use common readable formats such as PDF, XLSX, CSV or PNG.

3. Review and approval before publication

  1. The owner drafts or revises the document in Verity Documents. Drafts are not used as working instructions.
  2. The owner assigns approval tiers. Tier 1 is <Default tier 1 approvers, for example the ISMS owner>. Policies also need Tier 2, <Default tier 2 approvers, for example the CEO>. Each tier can name users, roles or groups: a named user must decide personally, and a role or group is satisfied when any one member approves.
  3. Assigning Tier 1 starts the review and notifies the approvers. Tier 2 starts once Tier 1 approves. Any rejection returns the document to draft with the approver's comment.
  4. When the final tier approves, Verity publishes the new version. The author of a change does not approve it. Verity does not stop an author from approving a tier they are assigned to. When the author is a named approver or belongs to an approving role or group, the owner names a different approver for that tier, for example <Alternate tier 1 approver when the ISMS owner is the author>. The ISMS owner checks the approval history for self-approvals during the annual confirmation described in Roles and Responsibilities.

4. Versions and changes

  1. Every content change creates a new version and goes through section 3. An editorial change that does not alter meaning, such as a typo or a contact detail, needs Tier 1 approval only.
  2. The owner updates the revision history for each version.
  3. Verity keeps earlier versions in the document's version history. Only the latest published version is in force. Superseded versions are kept for reference and retention, not for use.
  4. Printed or downloaded copies are uncontrolled. Anyone who relies on a copy checks it against the published version in Verity first.

5. Distribution and access

  1. Published documents are available to all staff in Verity. Rights to edit, approve and manage documents are granted by role in Verity and reviewed in the user access review.
  2. The owner runs an acknowledgement campaign in Verity Documents when a policy is first published, when it changes materially and <Acknowledgement frequency for policies, for example annually>, targeting the users, roles or groups it applies to. As part of the onboarding checklist, each new joiner is added to an acknowledgement campaign for the current policies and acknowledges them within <Number of days after start date to acknowledge policies> days of starting.
  3. Verity reminds recipients automatically. The document owner escalates acknowledgements still outstanding after <Number of days before escalating an overdue acknowledgement> days to the person's manager and records the escalation as a comment on the campaign.
  4. Documents are shared outside {{company_name}} only by the owner or the ISMS owner, in line with the Data Management Policy and, where needed, under a confidentiality agreement.

6. Storage, protection and readability

  1. Verity is the controlled store for ISMS documents and evidence. Records produced in other business systems, such as change tickets and build results, stay in those systems and are sampled into Verity as evidence. The owner of each such system sets its retention to at least the period in section 7, or exports the records to Verity Evidence before the system deletes them, because some tools delete logs and build results after 90 days by default. Records are never kept only in personal drives, email or chat.
  2. Records are not altered after they are filed. A correction is made by adding a new file or version with a note explaining the change, never by overwriting the original.
  3. Changes to documents, approvals and evidence are recorded in the Verity audit log.
  4. <Name and job title of the person responsible for storage checks> confirms <Frequency of storage checks, for example annually> that every location listed in the Documents register is backed up and that a sample of older records can still be opened and read.

7. Retention and disposal

InformationMinimum retention
Superseded policies and procedures<Retention period for superseded documents, for example seven years>
Risk assessments, Statements of Applicability, internal audit and management review records<Retention period for ISMS records, for example the current certification cycle plus three years>
Evidence attached to controls, change and incident records<Retention period for operating evidence, for example three years>
Training and acknowledgement records<Retention period for personnel records, for example employment plus two years>
  1. Where a law, regulation or contract requires a longer period, the longer period applies. The ISMS owner records these in the compliance obligations register.
  2. A legal hold, notified by <Role that issues legal holds, for example legal counsel>, suspends disposal for the records it names until it is lifted in writing.
  3. When a retention period ends, the record owner proposes disposal, the ISMS owner approves it, and the disposal (what, when, how and by whom) is recorded on a task in Verity Tasks before the task is closed. Verity keeps document versions and evidence items, and a workspace cannot delete them. Documents that are no longer needed are archived in Verity Documents. Where a law or contract requires a record held in Verity to be destroyed, for example personal data, the ISMS owner asks <Contact who handles deletion requests for the Verity workspace> to delete it and attaches the confirmation to the task.

8. Documents of external origin

  1. External documents the ISMS relies on are identified with their source, version or date and owner. Supplier reports, certificates and contracts are kept on the vendor record in Verity Vendors. Other external documents, such as penetration test reports, are attached as evidence to the related control.
  2. The owner checks for a newer version <Frequency of checks for new versions of external documents, for example annually> and when a supplier report or certificate nears expiry.
  3. Licensed standards and paid reports are shared only within the terms of their license.

9. Operating procedures

  1. {{company_name}} documents the operating procedures needed to run in-scope systems securely, including at least backup and restore, deployment, access provisioning and removal, incident response runbooks, log and alert review, and key and secret rotation.
  2. Each operating procedure has an owner, is available to the people who perform it, and is reviewed whenever the system it describes changes and at least annually.
  3. Procedures needed during an outage, such as restore and incident runbooks, also have a copy at <Location of the offline copy of critical runbooks> that can be reached when primary systems are down.

10. Periodic review

  1. Every document has a review date in Verity Documents. The default is 12 months from publication unless <Shorter review interval for specific documents, if any> applies.
  2. Before the review date the owner reviews the document against current practice and either confirms it unchanged or revises it. Either way the owner updates the review dates and revision history and takes the new version through Tier 1 approval, so the review is recorded even when nothing else changes.
  3. The ISMS owner reports documents past their review date at each management review.

[Optional] For regulated financial institutions: apply the record retention periods set by <Name of the financial regulator> and applicable banking law, have board-mandated policies approved by <Name of the board or board committee that approves policies> as the final tier, and keep records required for regulatory examination in storage that prevents alteration.

[Optional] For an on-premises estate or paper records: label printed controlled copies with their version, keep them in a locked location with a named custodian, replace them when a new version is published, and destroy retired copies by cross-cut shredding or a certified destruction service.

[Optional] For a card data environment: keep under this procedure the policies and operating procedures that each PCI DSS requirement asks for, and the roles assigned to carry them out. Review the information security policy at least once every 12 months and when the environment changes, keep each procedure current and known to the people who use it, and record who holds each assigned role.

Records and Evidence

RecordWhere it is kept in Verity
Documents register, versions, approvals and review datesVerity Documents, with changes in the audit log (controls GOV-28 and GOV-17)
Annual confirmation of required documents, self-approval check and review outcomesEvidence attached to controls GOV-28 and GOV-01
Acknowledgement campaign results and escalationsVerity Documents campaigns, with a yearly summary attached as evidence to control CS-04
Access and storage check resultsEvidence attached to control GOV-28
Disposal records and deletion confirmationsClosed tasks in Verity Tasks

Records in this table follow the retention periods in section 7.

Exceptions

A departure from this procedure is approved in advance by the ISMS owner, recorded as a risk in the Verity risk register with an acceptance and expiry date, and reported at the next management review.

Review

The ISMS owner reviews this procedure at least annually and earlier when the document store or approval workflow changes, when a new legal or contractual retention requirement arises, or after an audit finding on document control.

Related Documents

  • Information Security Policy
  • Data Management Policy
  • Information Security Roles and Responsibilities Policy
  • Third-Party Management Policy
  • Risk Assessment and Treatment Methodology
  • Change Management Procedure

title: Internal Audit Procedure and Program
summary: How internal audits are planned, staffed, sampled, reported and followed up, with a program that covers the whole ISMS scope each cycle.
content_html:
Internal Audit Procedure and Program

Document Type: Procedure

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the procedure owner>Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Purpose

This procedure sets out how {{company_name}} plans, performs, reports and follows up internal audits of its information security management system (ISMS), giving top management an objective, evidence based view of whether the ISMS works as written. It supports ISO/IEC 27001 clause 9.2, Annex A control A.5.35, SOC 2 criterion CC4.1 and Verity control GOV-13. It does not by itself make {{company_name}} compliant or certified.

Scope

  • Every ISMS process under ISO/IEC 27001 clauses 4 to 10, and every Annex A control marked applicable in the Statement of Applicability in Verity Frameworks.
  • Teams, locations, systems and suppliers in the ISMS scope on the Frameworks Scope page. Supplier operated controls are audited through the supplier assurance held in Vendors.
  • SOC 2 controls, where {{company_name}} also reports against SOC 2. One audit may serve both frameworks, but every control in the SOC 2 scope is evaluated at least once in each 12 months and within each SOC 2 audit period, as control GOV-13 requires, even where the ISO/IEC 27001 cycle is longer.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • Top management (<Name and job title of the executive sponsor>): approves the audit program, provides its resources and receives every audit report.
  • Audit program manager (<Name and job title of the audit program manager>): maintains the program, appoints auditors, approves audit plans and reports status to management review.
  • Lead auditor: plans and performs each audit, writes the report and verifies closure of findings.
  • Auditees (process and control owners): provide access, people and evidence on time, and own the correction of findings in their area.

Procedure

1. Audit program

  1. The program in Appendix A covers the clause 4 to 10 processes every year, and every applicable Annex A control at least once in each audit cycle of <Audit cycle length, for example 12 or 36 months>. The whole ISMS scope is audited before the first certification audit.
  2. An area is audited yearly, whatever its place in the cycle, when it carries high residual risk, its last audit found a nonconformity, it changed significantly, or an incident affected it. A significant change to the ISMS scope, the organization or the way information security is managed also triggers an independent review of the affected areas within <Months after a significant change to review the affected areas, for example six months>, added to the program as an unplanned audit.
  3. The program manager reviews the program <Program review frequency, for example quarterly> and after any trigger listed under Review. Top management approves it at the start of each cycle and after each change, through the approval tier on this document in Documents.
  4. Each planned audit is a task in Tasks owned by the lead auditor and due in the planned quarter, so a late audit shows as overdue.
  5. Methods include document review, interviews, observation, inspection of system settings, re-performance and review of Verity check results. An automated result supports a conclusion only once confirmed by another method.
  6. Between audits, each control owner confirms that their area follows the policies and procedures that apply to it at least <Frequency of owner compliance checks, for example every six months>, through a recurring task in Tasks that records what was checked, the sample and the result. Each shortfall is raised as an issue under the Corrective Action and Improvement Procedure. The program manager reviews these results when planning each audit.

[Optional] For a card data environment: the program tests that the PCI DSS scope was confirmed at least every 12 months and after each significant change (PCI DSS v4.0.1 requirement 12.5.2), or every six months for service providers (12.5.2.1), and, for service providers, that the quarterly reviews under 12.4.2 took place and were recorded (12.4.2.1). The auditor tests these activities and does not perform them.

2. Auditor objectivity and competence

  1. No auditor audits their own work, a process they manage, or work they performed or managed in the previous 12 months.
  2. Each auditor has completed <Minimum auditor qualification, for example an ISO/IEC 27001 internal auditor or lead auditor course> and understands the area audited. Technical specialists may support but not lead an audit.
  3. Before each audit, every auditor declares any conflict of interest in writing, and the program manager replaces an auditor who has one.
  4. Where no independent person is available, {{company_name}} uses <Source of independent auditors, for example an external audit firm>. The internal audit process is audited by someone who does not manage the program.
  5. The program manager keeps each auditor's competence record: training, experience and audits performed.

[Optional] For regulated financial institutions: <Board audit committee or equivalent> approves the program, the internal audit function performs or oversees ISMS audits and reports to that committee, and the program covers <Applicable regulation or supervisory guidance, for example DORA or the FFIEC IT Examination Handbook>. Each major nonconformity is assessed for reporting to <Name of the regulator>. Auditors who lead audits of technology areas hold a recognized IT audit qualification such as CISA. Where {{company_name}} uses SWIFT, the program schedules the independent assessment that supports the yearly Customer Security Programme attestation.

3. Planning each audit

  1. The lead auditor sends the auditees an audit plan at least <Audit plan notice period, for example 10 business days> before fieldwork, stating the objective, scope (requirements, controls, teams, locations, systems and period), criteria, methods, sampling, schedule and evidence requested.
  2. The criteria are {{company_name}} policies and procedures, the applicable ISO/IEC 27001 requirements and Statement of Applicability decisions, legal and contractual obligations in scope and, where relevant, SOC 2 criteria.
  3. The program manager approves the plan, which is attached to the audit task.
  4. Any test on a live system, whether by an internal auditor, the certification body, a customer auditor or a penetration tester, is agreed in writing with the system owner in advance, stating the systems, the tests, the access needed and the timing. Access is read only where possible. Anything beyond read only is carried out by a system administrator, not by the auditor. Tests that could affect availability run outside business hours or in an agreed window. Audit accounts are logged, time limited and removed when the test ends, and the written agreement is attached to the audit task.

[Optional] For an on-premises estate: each data center, server room and network room in scope is visited at least once per cycle, and samples are taken directly from systems that Verity checks do not cover.

4. Sampling

  1. The auditor, not the auditee, selects samples from the full population drawn from its source system, and records how they were chosen.
  2. Unless the plan justifies another size, the minimum sample for a control performed yearly is 1, quarterly 2, monthly 2, weekly 5, daily 15, and many times a day 25. A smaller population is tested in full.
  3. When a sample item fails, the auditor raises a finding or extends the sample to learn whether the failure is isolated, and records the decision.

5. Performing the audit

  1. Auditors keep working papers for every test: what was examined, the sample, the result and a reference to the evidence.
  2. Each finding states the requirement, the evidence observed and how it falls short. A finding without evidence is not reported.
  3. At a closing meeting the lead auditor presents the findings and their classes. Auditees may add evidence within <Days for auditee response, for example five business days>, after which the findings are final.

6. Classifying findings

ClassMeaningRecorded in Verity as
Major nonconformityA requirement is not addressed, a process or control has stopped working, several minor nonconformities show one area failing, or customer data or a legal or contractual obligation is exposed.Issue in Tasks, severity high, or critical where customer data is exposed now
Minor nonconformityA single lapse or partial gap that does not stop the requirement being met overall.Issue in Tasks, severity medium
ObservationNo requirement is breached yet, but a weakness could become a nonconformity if left alone.Issue in Tasks, severity low
Opportunity for improvementA way to make a working process better.Entry in the improvement log in Tasks (control GOV-30)

7. Reporting

  1. The lead auditor issues the report within <Days to issue the audit report, for example 10 business days> of the closing meeting, stating scope, criteria, period, auditors and their independence, methods and samples, a conclusion, each finding with its class and evidence, and any limits on the audit.
  2. The report goes to the auditees, the program manager and top management, and is attached as evidence to control GOV-13.
  3. Each finding is raised in Tasks within five business days, titled with the audit reference first, for example "IA-2027-02:", so one search finds them all. The lead auditor then closes the audit task.
  4. The program manager presents audit results and program status at each management review.

8. Follow up

  1. Each nonconformity and observation is handled under the Corrective Action and Improvement Procedure, with the owner of the audited process as issue owner.
  2. For each major and minor nonconformity, an auditor independent of the action verifies it and sets each corrective action on the issue to Verified before the issue is closed.
  3. The program manager reports nonconformities past their SLA to top management and the next management review.
  4. The next audit of the same area checks that earlier corrective actions still work.

Records and Evidence

RecordWhere it is kept in Verity
Approved audit programThis document in Documents, with its approval record
Audit plan, conflict declarations and working papersAttached to the audit task in Tasks, and as evidence to control GOV-13
Auditor competence records and audit reportsEvidence on control GOV-13
Findings, actions and verificationIssues in Tasks, with owner, severity, SLA, actions and status history
Change history of these recordsVerity audit log

Audit records are kept for <Retention period for audit records, for example three years> and at least for the certification cycle in which they were created.

Exceptions

Moving an audit to another quarter needs the program manager's approval, recorded with the reason on the audit task. Moving it further, or out of the cycle, needs top management approval. No exception may leave a clause 4 to 10 process unaudited for over 12 months, an applicable Annex A control unaudited in its cycle, or a control in the SOC 2 scope unevaluated in a SOC 2 audit period.

Review

The procedure owner reviews this procedure and the program every 12 months, using the review date in Documents, and earlier after a nonconformity in the audit process, a significant change to the ISMS scope, organization or auditors, a new ISO/IEC 27001 version, or a regulator or certification body request.

Related Documents

  • Information Security Policy
  • Information Security Roles and Responsibilities Policy
  • Risk Management Policy
  • Third-Party Management Policy
  • Management Review Procedure and Minutes
  • Corrective Action and Improvement Procedure

Appendix A: Audit Program

Cycle means once per audit cycle, or yearly when section 1, step 2 applies or the control is in the SOC 2 scope. Annex A controls excluded in the Statement of Applicability are not audited, but their exclusion reasons are checked in row 2.

Audit areaISO/IEC 27001 coverageFrequencyQuarter and auditor
1. Context, scope, leadership and policy4.1 to 4.4, 5.1 to 5.3, A.5.1 to A.5.4Yearly<Quarter and auditor>

title: Management Review Procedure and Minutes
summary: How top management reviews the ISMS: timing, attendees, required inputs, recorded decisions and tracked actions, with a minutes template.
content_html:
Management Review Procedure and Minutes

Document Type: Procedure

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the procedure owner>Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Purpose

This procedure sets out how top management of {{company_name}} reviews the information security management system (ISMS): when, who attends, what information they consider, what they decide, and how decisions are recorded and carried through. It supports ISO/IEC 27001 clauses 5.1 and 9.3, SOC 2 criteria CC1.2, CC2.2 and CC4.2, and Verity control GOV-15. It does not by itself make {{company_name}} compliant or certified.

Scope

  • The whole ISMS as recorded on the Scope page in Verity Frameworks, including controls operated by suppliers.
  • Every management review: full, interim or triggered (section 1).
  • A review may sit inside another leadership meeting if the agenda in section 2 is covered and its minutes are kept separately.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • Chair (<Name and job title of the executive who chairs the review>): a member of top management who runs the review, states its conclusion and approves the minutes.
  • Required attendees (<Job titles of required attendees, for example CEO, CTO and Head of People>): attend, or send a delegate who can decide for them.
  • ISMS owner (<Name and job title of the ISMS owner>): schedules the review, prepares the input pack, writes the minutes and tracks every action.
  • Input owners (risk owners, objective owners, the audit program manager and control owners): supply and present their inputs on time.
  • Action owners: complete actions by their due date and report status at the next review.

Procedure

1. Frequency and scheduling

  1. A full review covering every agenda item in section 2 is held at least every 12 months and before each certification or surveillance audit.
  2. Interim reviews are held at least every three months, as control GOV-15 requires, and cover at least agenda items 1, 4, 5 and 9.
  3. A triggered review is held within <Days to hold a triggered review, for example 30 days> of a major incident, a major nonconformity, a significant change to the ISMS scope, organization, ownership or key suppliers, or a new legal or contractual requirement with significant security impact. It covers the trigger and the agenda items it affects.
  4. The ISMS owner schedules each review as a recurring task in Tasks, due on the meeting date, so a missed review shows as overdue.
  5. A quorum is the chair, or a deputy from top management named by the chair, plus <Quorum, for example two of the required attendees>. Without a quorum the meeting may discuss but not decide, and the review is rescheduled within 30 days.

2. Agenda and inputs

  1. The ISMS owner sends the input pack to attendees at least <Days before the meeting to send the input pack, for example five business days> before the meeting. The pack states the date its figures were taken from Verity, and each figure shows the current period and the three before it so the direction of change is visible.
  2. The agenda is:
ItemWhat is presentedSource in Verity
1. Earlier actionsStatus of every action from earlier reviews, with reasons for any that are lateTasks, searched by review reference
2. ContextChanges in the internal and external factors that shape the ISMSEvidence on control GOV-24
3. Interested partiesNew or changed requirements of customers, regulators, suppliers, staff and ownersEvidence on controls GOV-25 and GOV-05
4. Nonconformities and corrective actionsIssues raised, closed, overdue and repeated, root cause themes, and actions verified as effectiveIssues in Tasks
5. Monitoring and measurementControl check results, failing or stale evidence, incidents, and measures against their targetsFrameworks dashboard, Evidence and Tasks
6. AuditsInternal, certification body and customer audit results, penetration test results, and audit program statusEvidence on controls GOV-13 and GOV-16
7. Security objectivesProgress of each objective against its target and dateEvidence on control GOV-26
8. FeedbackCustomer questionnaires and complaints, regulator contact, supplier notices and staff suggestionsInput owners, with Tasks and Vendors records
9. RiskRisk assessment results, new and changed risks, risks above appetite, overdue treatment actions and acceptances near expiryRisk register
10. ImprovementOpen proposals, and completed improvements with a sample checked for effectImprovement log in Tasks, control GOV-30
11. ResourcesWhether people, time, tools and budget are enough for the plan and objectivesInput owners

[Optional] For a card data environment: item 5 includes the PCI DSS compliance status: the date of the last scope confirmation, the internal and approved scanning vendor (ASV) external scan results for the last four quarters with any failed scan and its passing rescan, open findings from the last assessment, and the date the next assessment is due. For service providers, the review confirms the executive accountable for the PCI DSS compliance program and the program charter (PCI DSS v4.0.1 requirement 12.4.1), and receives the results of the quarterly reviews under requirement 12.4.2.

[Optional] For an on-premises estate: item 11 includes hardware and software near end of support, data center capacity, and physical security events at each site.

3. Conducting the review

  1. The chair confirms the quorum, and the minutes record attendees, delegates and absentees.
  2. Each agenda item is presented and given a recorded conclusion, including "no change" where that applies. A full review does not skip any item.
  3. The chair states an overall conclusion: whether the ISMS still fits the business, has enough resources and is achieving its objectives, with reasons where it is not.

4. Decisions and outputs

  1. The minutes record each decision on improvements; changes to the ISMS, including its scope, policies, objectives, risk appetite or the Statement of Applicability; resources; and risks, including any acceptance of a risk above appetite.
  2. Every decision that needs work becomes a task in Tasks within five business days, with an owner, a due date and a title starting with the review reference, for example "MR-2027-Q1:".
  3. A risk acceptance takes effect only when the risk owner records it in the risk register with the reason and an expiry date.
  4. A decided change to the ISMS is made as a planned change: documents through a new version and approval in Documents, and applicability decisions in the Statement of Applicability in Frameworks.
  5. An action still open at two reviews in a row is escalated by the chair to <Escalation point for actions late across two reviews, for example the CEO or the board>. An action is closed only with evidence that the work was done, or cancelled by the chair with a recorded reason.
  6. After each full review, the ISMS owner sends a written summary of the conclusion, decisions and significant risks to <Oversight body, for example the board or its audit or risk committee> within <Days to report to the oversight body, for example 30 days>. That body's own minutes record that it considered the summary, the questions it raised and any decisions it made.

[Optional] For regulated financial institutions: the oversight body in step 6 is the board or a board committee such as the audit or risk committee. The review also covers supervisory examination results and open regulator findings, and the minutes record any matter reportable to <Name of the regulator> and the date it was reported. The board or its committee approves the information security policy and the risk appetite at least every 12 months, and its minutes are attached as evidence to control GOV-02.

5. Minutes

  1. The ISMS owner circulates draft minutes, using Appendix A, within <Days to circulate minutes, for example five business days> of the review.
  2. The chair approves the minutes within five business days of receiving them. The approved minutes and the input pack are attached as evidence to control GOV-15.
  3. Decisions that change what staff must do are communicated by a campaign in Documents asking staff to acknowledge the changed document, or through <Internal communication channel for other decisions>.

Records and Evidence

RecordWhere it is kept in Verity
Input pack and approved minutesEvidence on control GOV-15
Actions from each reviewTasks, with owner, due date and status history
Risk acceptancesRisk register, with reason and expiry date
Changes to documents and applicability decisionsDocuments version history and approvals; the Statement of Applicability in Frameworks
Summary sent to the oversight body, and that body's minutes showing it was consideredEvidence on control GOV-02
Change history of these recordsVerity audit log

Management review records are kept for <Retention period for management review records, for example three years>, and at least for the certification cycle in which they were created.

Exceptions

A full review may not be skipped. If a scheduled review cannot be held, the ISMS owner records the reason on the review task and the review is held within 30 days. An interim review may be merged into a full review held in the same period. The chair may delegate chairing to a deputy from top management, and the minutes name the deputy.

Review

The procedure owner reviews this procedure every 12 months, using the review date in Documents, and earlier after a finding about management review from an internal or certification audit, a change in top management, a significant change to the ISMS scope, or a new ISO/IEC 27001 version.

Related Documents

  • Information Security Policy
  • Information Security Roles and Responsibilities Policy
  • Risk Management Policy
  • Incident Response Plan
  • Internal Audit Procedure and Program
  • Corrective Action and Improvement Procedure

Appendix A: Management Review Minutes

Copy this appendix for each review. Fill every cell; write "None" rather than leaving a cell empty.

2. Context
3. Interested parties
4. Nonconformities and corrective actions

11. Resources
Overall conclusion: does the ISMS still fit the business, have enough resources and achieve its objectives?

title: Corrective Action and Improvement Procedure
summary: How nonconformities are raised, corrected, traced to root cause, fixed and verified in Tasks, and how ISMS improvements are logged and decided.
content_html:
Corrective Action and Improvement Procedure

Document Type: Procedure

Company Name:{{company_name}}
Document Owner:<Name and job title of the procedure owner>Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date:<Effective date>Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review:<Date of last review>Next Review: <Date of next review>

Purpose

This procedure sets out how {{company_name}} records and fixes nonconformities in its information security management system (ISMS), removes their causes so they do not recur, checks that the fixes worked, and tracks improvements to the ISMS. It supports ISO/IEC 27001 clauses 10.1 and 10.2, SOC 2 criterion CC4.2, and Verity controls GOV-08, GOV-30 and LM-05. It does not by itself make {{company_name}} compliant or certified.

Scope

  • Every nonconformity in the ISMS scope recorded on the Scope page in Verity Frameworks, from any source, including those in controls operated by suppliers.
  • Every proposal to improve the ISMS.
  • Security incidents are first handled under the Incident Response Plan. This procedure covers the control failures and lessons an incident reveals.

Roles and Responsibilities

  • ISMS owner (<Name and job title of the ISMS owner>): triages every issue, approves corrective action plans, runs the improvement log and reports trends to management review.
  • Issue owner: the owner of the process or control where the nonconformity occurred. Accountable for correction, root cause analysis, corrective action and closure evidence.
  • Assignees: carry out the actions under an issue.
  • Verifier: a person who did not carry out the actions, such as an internal auditor or the ISMS owner, who confirms they were completed and effective.
  • Top management: provides resources, decides escalations and receives the trend report.
  • All staff: report suspected nonconformities.

Procedure

1. Terms

  • Nonconformity: a requirement that is not met. Requirements include {{company_name}} policies, procedures and controls, legal and contractual obligations, and the ISO/IEC 27001 requirements in scope.
  • Correction: action that fixes the instance found.
  • Corrective action: action that removes the cause, so the problem does not happen again or elsewhere.
  • Improvement: a change that makes the ISMS more effective or efficient when nothing has failed.

2. Sources

Nonconformities are found through internal audits; certification body, customer and regulator audits; security incidents and their postmortems; failed control checks, which the "Control check failed" automation in Tasks raises as issues owned by the control owner; stale evidence; vulnerabilities past their remediation deadline; risks above appetite; monitoring alerts; complaints and customer feedback; supplier reviews; management review; and staff reports.

3. Raising and triage

  1. Anyone who finds a suspected nonconformity raises an issue in Tasks, or reports it to the ISMS owner, within <Time to raise an issue, for example one business day>.
  2. The issue records the requirement not met, the evidence, the source, the date detected, the category, and the impact and urgency that set its severity.
  3. The ISMS owner triages each new issue within <Triage time, for example two business days>: confirms it is a nonconformity, confirms the owner and severity, and records the reason for any severity override. An item that is neither a nonconformity nor an audit observation is cancelled with the reason, or moved to the improvement log.
  4. Audit findings keep the class the auditor gave them: a major nonconformity is high severity, or critical where customer data is exposed now; a minor nonconformity is medium; an observation is low. For a finding raised by the certification body, a customer or a regulator, the issue records the deadline that party set for correction and for the corrective action plan. Where that deadline is earlier than the resolve time, it becomes the issue's due date, and the ISMS owner sends the plan to that party before the deadline.
  5. At triage the ISMS owner gives each issue the SLA level that matches its severity: <SLA level for each issue severity, for example critical P1, high P2, medium P3, low P4>. The resolve time for each SLA level is set in Tasks settings to <Resolve time for each SLA level, for example P1 7 days, P2 30 days, P3 60 days, P4 90 days>. Verity does not set the SLA level from the severity, and an issue without one has no SLA deadline, so triage is not complete until the level is set. The clock runs until the issue is closed, including while it is under review, and pauses only while the issue is blocked. Moving an issue to blocked needs the reason in a comment. Verity notifies the owner and assignees as the deadline nears and when it passes.

[Optional] For a card data environment: a failure of a critical security control system, such as logging, intrusion detection, anti-malware, file integrity monitoring, access control or segmentation, is raised at critical or high severity and handled to meet PCI DSS v4.0.1 requirements 10.7.2 and 10.7.3. The issue records the start and end date and time of the failure, its cause, any security events during the failure and how they were handled, whether further action is needed, the action taken to stop it recurring, and when monitoring resumed.

4. Correction

  1. The issue owner contains and corrects the nonconformity within <Time to complete correction for each severity, for example critical 24 hours and high three business days>, recorded as a containment action on the issue.
  2. The owner assesses the consequences: whether customer data, a contractual commitment or other systems were affected. Where they were, the owner raises an incident under the Incident Response Plan and records its reference on the issue.

5. Root cause analysis

  1. Every issue records a cause statement. A full root cause analysis, using five whys or a cause and effect diagram, is completed within <Days to complete root cause analysis, for example 10 business days> for critical and high issues and for any repeat of the same nonconformity within 12 months.
  2. The analysis asks why the nonconformity happened and why it was not detected sooner. "Human error" is not accepted as a cause on its own: the analysis states what allowed the error.
  3. The owner checks other teams, systems and controls that work the same way for the same problem, and records what was checked and found. Each similar nonconformity found is raised as its own issue.

6. Corrective action

  1. The owner records each corrective action, and any preventive action for similar areas, as an action on the issue with an owner and a due date. Actions are sized to the harm the nonconformity caused or could cause.
  2. The ISMS owner approves the plan in a comment on the issue before work starts. Where no action is proportionate, the reason is recorded and the remaining risk goes to the risk register.
  3. Where an action will take longer than the resolve time, the ISMS owner approves a new date and any interim measure in a comment on the issue. A second extension for a critical or high issue needs top management approval.
  4. Where the cause lies in the ISMS itself, the change is made as a planned change: policies and procedures through a new version and approval in Documents, applicability decisions in the Statement of Applicability in Frameworks, and risks in the risk register.

[Optional] For an on-premises estate: actions that change infrastructure go through change approval (control SD-01) in an agreed change window, and verification includes a check on the device or system itself, not only its record.

7. Verification and closure

  1. When all actions are complete, the issue moves to under review. The verifier checks that the work was done and that the next operation of the control, or a re-test where the control runs rarely, shows the nonconformity has not recurred. The verifier then sets each corrective action to Verified, which records the verifier's name and the date. The verifier is never the issue owner or the owner of the action being verified. Critical and high issues and every audit nonconformity have Requires approval switched on at triage, so they can be closed only after the verifier approves them while they are under review. Verity does not block self-verification, so at each overdue review the ISMS owner checks the verifier names on issues closed since the last review.
  2. The issue is closed with a closure note that references the evidence. Evidence is attached to the issue and, where it shows a control operating, also as evidence on that control.
  3. If verification fails, the issue returns to in progress and the root cause analysis is repeated.
  4. No issue is closed on the owner's word alone.

[Optional] For regulated financial institutions: issues raised by <Name of the regulator> or by the internal audit function are closed only after validation by the internal audit function, overdue high and critical issues are reported to <Board audit or risk committee, or equivalent> at each meeting, and each issue records any regulatory reporting deadline.

8. Escalation and reporting

  1. The ISMS owner reviews <Overdue review frequency, for example weekly> the issues past their SLA deadline or due date, the issues that are blocked, and any issue with no SLA level, and escalates critical and high ones to top management.
  2. Before each management review, the ISMS owner prepares a trend summary: issues raised, closed, overdue and repeated, by source and severity, with root cause themes. It is attached as evidence to control GOV-08 and presented at the review.

9. Improvement log

  1. Improvement proposals from audits, incidents, measurement results, management review, customer feedback and staff are recorded as tasks in Tasks with a title starting "Improvement:". A shared saved view named "Improvement log" lists them.
  2. The ISMS owner decides on each proposal within <Days to decide on an improvement proposal, for example 30 days>, weighing benefit against effort, and records the decision and reason in a comment.
  3. Accepted proposals get an owner and a due date, and close only with evidence that the change was made. Rejected proposals are cancelled with the reason.
  4. Management review checks a sample of completed improvements for their effect.

Records and Evidence

RecordWhere it is kept in Verity
Nonconformity: requirement, evidence, source, severity, owner and datesIssue in Tasks, with its status history
Cause statement and root cause analysisOn the issue, with any working files attached
Containment, corrective, preventive and verification actionsActions on the issue, with owner, due date and verifier
Approvals, extensions and decisionsComments on the issue or improvement task
Closure evidenceAttached to the issue, and as evidence on the affected control
Remaining risk from nonconformities not fully correctedRisk register, with treatment or acceptance and expiry date
Improvement logTasks, saved view "Improvement log"
Trend summaryEvidence on control GOV-08
Change history of these recordsVerity audit log

These records are kept for <Retention period for nonconformity records, for example three years> after closure, and at least for the certification cycle in which they were created.

Exceptions

A nonconformity that cannot be corrected, for example because a supplier will not change, is closed only after its risk owner records a treatment, or an acceptance with an expiry date, in the risk register, and the issue references that risk. Any other departure from this procedure needs the ISMS owner's approval, recorded on the issue with the reason.

Review

The procedure owner reviews this procedure every 12 months, using the review date in Documents, and earlier after an audit finding about corrective action, a rise in repeat nonconformities, a change to severity levels, SLA levels or resolve times in Tasks, a significant organizational change, or a new ISO/IEC 27001 version.

Related Documents

  • Information Security Policy
  • Incident Response Plan
  • Risk Management Policy
  • Operations Security Policy
  • Internal Audit Procedure and Program
  • Management Review Procedure and Minutes

title: Acceptable Use Policy
summary: Rules for using company information, systems, email, internet, AI tools and devices, with monitoring, reporting, yearly acknowledgement and consequences.
content_html:
Acceptable Use Policy

Company Name: {{company_name}}
Document Owner: <Name and job title of the policy owner> Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date: <Effective date> Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review: <Date of last review> Next Review: <Date of next review>

1. Purpose

This policy sets the rules for using {{company_name}} information, systems and devices: what is allowed, what is prohibited, what is monitored, how to report problems and what happens when rules are broken.

2. Scope

  • Employees, contractors, temporary staff and third parties who hold a {{company_name}} account or handle {{company_name}} information ("users").
  • All company information in any form, and all company systems, devices and services.
  • Personally owned devices whenever they are used to reach company information or systems.

Classification and handling rules are in the Data Management Policy, and rules for working away from the office are in the Remote Working Policy. In this policy, "Confidential information" means information classified Confidential or Restricted under the Data Management Policy.

3. Roles and Responsibilities

Role Responsibilities
Policy owner (named in the header) Maintains this policy, runs acknowledgement campaigns, handles exception requests and reports acknowledgement and breach figures to management review.
People team Makes compliance with this policy a term of employment and contractor agreements, and runs the disciplinary process.
Managers Confirm staff have acknowledged this policy before requesting their access, and report suspected breaches.
IT and security team Operate the enforcing technical controls, keep the approved software and AI tool lists current, and review monitoring.
Users Follow this policy, acknowledge it when asked and report anything listed in section 6.

4. Acceptable Use Rules

4.1 General use

  1. Company systems are used for {{company_name}} business. Occasional personal use is allowed when it does not interfere with work and breaks no rule in this policy.
  2. Users access only what their role requires and was granted under the Access Control Policy, and report access they should not hold to IT within one business day.
  3. Information is handled according to its classification, and Confidential information is shared only with authorized people who need it for their work.
  4. Users lock their screen whenever they leave a device unattended, and do not leave Confidential papers on desks, printers or in meeting rooms.

4.2 Accounts and credentials

  1. Accounts, passwords, authentication devices and access tokens are personal and never shared or lent.
  2. Work passwords and shared credentials are stored only in <Name of the company password manager>. Credentials used by systems and services are kept in <Name of the secrets management tool>, and privileged and emergency credentials in <Name of the privileged access vault or the sealed emergency credential procedure>, as the Access Control Policy sets out. No credential is ever sent by email, chat, ticket or document.
  3. Users enroll in multi-factor authentication wherever it is offered, and never approve a sign-in request they did not start.
  4. A user who suspects a credential is exposed changes it at once and reports it under section 6.

4.3 Devices

  1. Company work is done on company devices enrolled in <Name of the device management tool>, and on personal phones only as rule 4.3.3 allows. Users never disable or bypass device management, encryption, screen lock, endpoint protection, web filtering or updates.
  2. Software is installed only from <Location of the approved software list or self-service catalog> or with written IT approval. Unlicensed or pirated software is never installed.
  3. Personal phones may be used for company email, chat and multi-factor authentication only when protected by <Management or app protection method required on personal phones>. Personal computers are never used to reach Confidential information or production systems.
  4. Company devices are not lent to family members or anyone else.

4.4 Email, messaging and sharing

  1. Company business is conducted only on company email, chat and file sharing accounts, and company information is never copied to personal email, storage or messaging apps.
  2. Confidential information leaves {{company_name}} only through <Approved method for sending Confidential information externally, for example links restricted to named recipients>, only to recipients covered by a contract or nondisclosure agreement, and never through public or "anyone with the link" shares.
  3. Unexpected attachments, links, credential requests and payment change requests are verified through a known contact route before any action.

4.5 Internet and public communication

  1. Users do not visit or download from sites hosting malware, illegal or pirated material, or content that breaches the Code of Conduct.
  2. Users do not post Confidential or Restricted information on social media, forums, public code or paste sites, and speak for {{company_name}} in public only when authorized.

4.6 AI tools

  1. Only approved AI tools are used for company work: the services recorded in Verity Vendors with the tag <Tag that marks AI services in Vendors, for example ai> and the status Approved or Active. Each one's data classification field records the highest classification it is cleared to receive. The list is published at <Location where staff can see the approved AI tools>.
  2. Customer data, personal data, credentials, source code and other Confidential information go only into an approved tool cleared for that classification, and only where the vendor contract excludes training on {{company_name}} data.
  3. Users check AI output for accuracy, security and licensing before relying on it, and remain accountable for what they use.
  4. AI assistants, extensions and plugins are not connected to company email, calendars, drives or repositories, and new AI tools are not used, until they pass vendor review under the Third-Party Management Policy.

4.7 Prohibited use

Users must never:

  • Access, or attempt to access, any account, system or data without authorization.
  • Scan or test the security of company or customer systems without written authorization from the security team.
  • Disable or bypass security controls, or use unapproved VPNs, proxies or remote access tools.
  • Copy company information to unapproved removable media, personal storage or personal accounts.
  • Use company systems for illegal activity, harassment, a personal business, cryptocurrency mining, bulk unsolicited messages or infringing intellectual property.
  • Connect unapproved devices to company networks or production systems.

[Optional] For a card data environment: full primary account numbers are never sent by email, chat or tickets, or stored outside systems approved for card data, and only end-user technologies on the list at <Location of the approved end-user technology list for the card data environment>, each approved with its permitted uses by <Role that approves end-user technologies for the card data environment>, are used (see PCI DSS Requirement 12.2.1).

[Optional] For regulated financial institutions: communications about <Regulated activities whose communications must be recorded, for example trading or client advice> use only recorded company channels, never personal phones or messaging apps. Workstations used to operate payment systems such as SWIFT or the core banking system are used for nothing else: no email, no general web browsing and no personal use.

[Optional] For on-premises estates: personal devices connect only to the guest network, and unknown USB devices are never plugged into company equipment.

5. Monitoring

  1. {{company_name}} monitors and logs use of company systems, devices, networks and accounts to protect information, detect misuse and meet legal duties, including sign-ins, web traffic from managed devices, file sharing, endpoint alerts and data leakage alerts.
  2. Users should not expect privacy in content created, stored or sent on company systems, to the extent permitted by <Employment and privacy laws that apply where users work>.
  3. Monitoring data is reviewed only by <Roles authorized to review monitoring data, for example the security team>. Reviewing a named individual's communications needs prior written approval from <Role that approves investigation of an individual, for example the head of people with legal counsel>, recorded on the investigation task.
  4. Monitoring data is deleted after <Retention period for monitoring logs, for example twelve months> unless an investigation or legal hold needs it.

6. Reporting

  1. Users report suspected security events, phishing, misdirected messages, exposed credentials and breaches of this policy immediately to <Security reporting channel, for example a security email address or chat channel>, and a lost or stolen device within <Time limit for reporting a lost or stolen device, for example one hour> of noticing.
  2. Good-faith reports are never penalized, even when wrong. The security team records each report and handles it under the Incident Response Plan.
  3. Concerns about misconduct that a user cannot raise with their manager go to <Confidential ethics or whistleblowing channel>.

7. Acknowledgement and Consequences

  1. New users acknowledge this policy during onboarding, through an acknowledgement campaign on this document in Verity Documents, before access to any system other than their sign-in account and Verity is granted. Every user is given a Verity account with <Verity role given to all staff so they can acknowledge documents, for example a custom role named Staff> so campaigns reach them. A user who cannot be given a Verity account acknowledges through <Alternative acknowledgement method, for example a signed form kept in the HR system>, and those records are attached as evidence to control CS-04.
  2. The policy owner runs an acknowledgement campaign for all users every twelve months, and within 30 days of publishing a version that changes a rule. Users have <Number of days users have to acknowledge, for example 14> days to respond.
  3. For each user who misses the deadline, the policy owner creates a task in Tasks for their manager. Access may be suspended until the user acknowledges.
  4. Breaches are handled under the disciplinary process in the Human Resource Security Policy, in proportion to seriousness and intent, up to termination of employment or contract. Access may be suspended during an investigation. Third-party breaches are handled under their contract.

8. Records and Evidence

Record Where it is kept
Approved versions of this policy and their approvals Verity Documents: version history and approval tiers of this document
Acknowledgement by each user Acknowledgement campaigns on this document; the yearly completion export is attached as evidence to controls CS-04 and GOV-04
Onboarding checklists showing acknowledgement before access Attached as evidence to control HR-06
Employment and contractor agreement templates that make this policy a condition of the engagement Attached as evidence to control HR-02
Reviewed web filtering and data leakage alerts Quarterly reports attached as evidence to controls EP-07 and DM-19
Breaches and disciplinary outcomes Case files stay in the HR system; a yearly anonymized summary is attached as evidence to control GOV-11
Exceptions A task in Tasks per exception, plus a Risk register entry where section 9 requires one

Records in this table are kept for <Retention period for records under this policy, for example three years> after they are superseded or closed. HR case files follow the People team's retention schedule.

9. Exceptions

  1. Exception requests go to the policy owner in writing, stating the rule, business reason, systems and data involved, duration and any compensating control.
  2. Exceptions are approved by <Role that approves exceptions to this policy>. No exception is granted to rules 4.2.1 and 4.2.2.
  3. Each approved exception is recorded as a task in Tasks with an owner and a due date equal to its expiry, no more than <Maximum length of an exception, for example six months> away. It lapses at expiry unless approved again.
  4. An exception that leaves a risk above <Risk score above which an exception needs a formal risk acceptance> is also recorded in the Risk register as an accepted risk with an acceptance expiry date.

10. Review

The policy owner reviews this policy at least every twelve months, using the review date on this document in Verity Documents. An earlier review follows adoption of a new class of tool, a serious misuse incident, a change in law affecting monitoring or personal devices, or an audit finding against this policy. Changes go through the document's approval tiers, and a changed rule starts a new acknowledgement campaign.

11. Related Documents

  • Information Security Policy
  • Data Management Policy
  • Access Control Policy
  • Code of Conduct
  • Human Resource Security Policy
  • Remote Working Policy
  • Third-Party Management Policy
  • Incident Response Plan
  • Competence and Awareness Procedure

12. Revision History

Version Date Author Description of change

title: Remote Working Policy
summary: Security rules for working from home, in public and while traveling: devices, connections, screen privacy, printing, lost devices and working abroad.
content_html:
Remote Working Policy

Company Name: {{company_name}}
Document Owner: <Name and job title of the policy owner> Version: <Version number, for example 1.0>
Effective Date: <Effective date> Approved By: <Name and job title of the approver>
Last Review: <Date of last review> Next Review: <Date of next review>

1. Purpose

This policy sets the rules that protect {{company_name}} information and devices when people work outside company premises: at home, at client sites, in shared or public spaces and while traveling.

2. Scope

  • Everyone who works for {{company_name}} outside company premises, whether full time, hybrid or occasionally, including contractors.
  • All company information handled there, and all company devices taken or used there.
  • All connections from outside company premises to company systems, including production and administrative access.

The Acceptable Use Policy applies everywhere and is not repeated here. This policy adds the rules that apply because the work happens away from the office. In this policy, "Confidential information" means information classified Confidential or Restricted under the Data Management Policy.

3. Roles and Responsibilities

Role Responsibilities
Policy owner Maintains this policy, handles exception requests under section 12 and runs the acknowledgement campaigns.
People team Records remote working arrangements and checks requests to work from another country with legal counsel.
Managers Approve remote working for their staff and confirm the role can be done securely away from the office.
IT team Issues and manages devices, runs remote access, provides support, and locks or wipes lost devices.
Security team Monitors remote access and device compliance, and handles reported events under the Incident Response Plan.
Remote workers Follow this policy, keep their working area and devices secure and report problems at once.

4. Eligibility and Approval

  1. Remote working is open to <Roles or groups eligible for remote working, for example all employees who have completed onboarding>, with approval from the person's manager. The People team records each arrangement in the HR system.
  2. Before working remotely for the first time, and every twelve months after, the person acknowledges this policy through an acknowledgement campaign on this document in Verity Documents. A person without a Verity account acknowledges through the alternative method set out in the Acceptable Use Policy.
  3. Working from another country for more than <Number of days abroad that needs approval, for example 10 working days a year> needs prior approval from the manager and <Role that approves working from another country, for example the head of people with legal counsel>, requested at least <Notice period for working abroad, for example 15 business days> ahead. The approval is recorded on a task in Tasks.
  4. Company devices are never taken to, and company systems are never accessed from, <Countries where remote work is not permitted, for example countries under sanctions or export restrictions that apply to the company>.

[Optional] For regulated financial institutions: staff carrying out <Regulated activities whose communications must be recorded, for example trading or client advice> work remotely only where their communications are recorded and their work can be supervised. Paper customer records are not taken home. Where a regulator expects notice of remote working arrangements for critical functions, <Role that notifies the regulator, for example the head of compliance> makes and records it. Payment systems such as SWIFT are not operated from outside company premises unless <Conditions under which remote operation of payment systems is allowed, for example a dedicated hardened device and approval by the head of operations>.

5. Devices

  1. Remote work is done only on company devices enrolled in <Name of the device management tool>, with full-disk encryption, endpoint protection, automatic updates and a screen lock after <Idle time before the screen locks, no more than 15 minutes>. Personal phones are used only as the Acceptable Use Policy allows.
  2. Access to company systems from outside company premises requires a device that passes the compliance checks in <Tool that checks device compliance at sign-in, for example the identity provider's conditional access>. A device that fails is blocked until IT resolves the cause.
  3. Company devices are used only by the person they were issued to, and are never left signed in where others can use them.
  4. Company information is not saved to personal USB storage or home network storage. Printing is covered by rule 7.6.

6. Connections

  1. Every sign-in to company systems uses multi-factor authentication. Production and administrative access from outside company premises goes only through <Approved remote access method, for example the zero trust access service or VPN>.
  2. Home Wi-Fi uses WPA2 or WPA3 encryption with a password that is not the router's default, and the router's admin password is changed from its default.
  3. On public or shared Wi-Fi, people connect only through <Approved remote access method, for example the zero trust access service or VPN> or a personal phone hotspot. Public or shared computers, such as hotel business center computers, are never used for company work.

[Optional] For a card data environment: any remote network access from outside company premises that could reach or affect the card data environment requires multi-factor authentication (see PCI DSS Requirement 8.4.3), and remote access is configured so that card data cannot be copied to the remote device unless a documented business need is approved (see PCI DSS Requirement 3.4.2). Personal devices never connect to the card data environment.

[Optional] For on-premises estates: on-premises systems are administered remotely only through <Jump host or privileged access tool used for remote administration>, with sessions recorded and a sample reviewed <Frequency of privileged session review, for example monthly> by <Role that reviews privileged sessions>, never through remote desktop exposed to the internet.

7. Working Conditions at Home and in Public

  1. Screens are placed so that others cannot read them. A privacy filter is used whenever working in a public space.
  2. Calls about Confidential matters are taken only where they cannot be overheard, with a headset in shared spaces and with voice assistants muted or out of range.
  3. Before sharing a screen, people close Confidential windows and notifications, and use a blurred or plain background on video.
  4. Screens are locked whenever the person steps away, including at home.
  5. Confidential paper is kept in a locked drawer or cabinet when not in use.
  6. Confidential information is printed outside company premises only where the person's remote working arrangement, approved and recorded under rule 4.1, allows it. Printed company material is destroyed with a cross-cut shredder or returned to the office for secure disposal, never put in household waste.

8. Travel and Devices Away from the Office

  1. Devices are carried as hand luggage and never left unattended in vehicles, public places or hotel rooms, unless locked in a room safe.
  2. Confidential paper and storage media are carried only when the work needs them, kept in a closed bag under the person's control, and never sent by ordinary post.
  3. For travel to <Countries for which staff must use a travel loaner device>, IT issues a loaner device with only the access the trip needs, and resets it on return.
  4. If a border or other official takes a device or demands access to it, the person reports it on arrival. IT treats the device as untrusted, checks or reimages it and resets the credentials it held.
  5. Company equipment other than laptops and phones, such as monitors and docking stations, is recorded by IT in Verity Assets, with the person as its custodian, when it is issued, and is returned, with its record updated, when they leave.

9. Lost or Stolen Devices

  1. A lost or stolen device is reported to <Security reporting channel, for example a security email address or chat channel> within <Time limit for reporting a lost or stolen device, for example one hour> of noticing, at any time of day. Theft is also reported to the police, and the reference is recorded.
  2. On a report, IT locks the device at once. If it is not recovered within <Time after which an unrecovered device is wiped, for example 24 hours>, IT wipes it, confirms the wipe completed, and resets passwords and sessions the device held.
  3. Each loss is recorded as a task in Tasks with an owner and due date. If the device was unencrypted, out of compliance, or may have exposed Confidential information, it is handled as an incident under the Incident Response Plan.

10. Support and Monitoring

  1. IT support is available through <IT support channel and hours>. Remote support sessions are started only by the user, through <Approved remote support tool>. IT never asks for a password, and people verify anyone who calls claiming to be IT through the support channel.
  2. {{company_name}} monitors remote sign-ins, remote access sessions and device compliance as described in the Acceptable Use Policy. Sign-ins from unexpected countries or unmanaged devices raise an alert to the security team.
  3. The security team reviews the device compliance report <Frequency of the device compliance review, for example monthly>. Each device out of compliance for longer than <Days a device may stay out of compliance, for example 7> days gets a task in Tasks for its user with a due date.

11. Records and Evidence

Record Where it is kept
Approved versions of this policy Verity Documents: version history and approval tiers of this document
Acknowledgement by each remote worker Acknowledgement campaigns on this document
Remote working arrangements and manager approvals, including permission to print Confidential information The HR system, kept by the People team
Approvals to work from another country A task in Tasks per request, with the decision recorded on it
Device compliance reports covering encryption, screen lock, updates and endpoint protection Attached each review period as evidence to controls EP-01, EP-02, EP-03, EP-04 and EP-06
Remote access configuration showing multi-factor authentication and device checks Attached yearly as evidence to controls NS-11 and IAM-03
Equipment issued for use away from the office, with the person who holds it Verity Assets, with the person recorded as custodian; a yearly export is attached as evidence to control LM-01
Lost device reports and wipe confirmations A task in Tasks per loss; wipe confirmations attached as evidence to control EP-05
Exceptions A task in Tasks per exception, plus a Risk register entry where rule 12.3 requires one

Records in this table are kept for <Retention period for records under this policy, for example three years> after they are superseded or closed.

12. Exceptions

  1. Exception requests go to the policy owner in writing, stating the rule, the reason, the duration and any compensating control.
  2. Exceptions are approved by <Role that approves exceptions to this policy> and recorded as a task in Tasks with an owner and a due date equal to the expiry, no more than <Maximum length of an exception, for example six months> away.
  3. An exception that leaves a risk above <Risk score above which an exception needs a formal risk acceptance> is also recorded in the Risk register as an accepted risk with an acceptance expiry date.
  4. No exception allows remote access without multi-factor authentication or from a country listed in rule 4.4.

13. Review

The policy owner reviews this policy at least every twelve months, using the review date on this document in Verity Documents. An earlier review follows a change of remote access technology or device management tool, an incident involving a remote device or connection, a change in the countries listed in rule 4.4, or an audit finding against this policy. A change to any rule starts a new acknowledgement campaign.

14. Related Documents

  • Acceptable Use Policy
  • Information Security Policy
  • Access Control Policy
  • Asset Management Policy
  • Data Management Policy
  • Cryptography Policy
  • Physical Security Policy
  • Human Resource Security Policy
  • Incident Response Plan

15. Revision History

Version Date Author Description of change
<Version number, for example 1.0> <Effective date> <Name and job title of the policy owner> First approved version.
